content_voiceover: RIPA, ristocetin-induced platelet agglutination, tests how well VWF bridges platelets via GPIb in response to increasing ristocetin concentrations. In normal plasma, you see a dose-dependent response, agglutination increases as ristocetin concentration rises from 0.8 up through 1.1 milligrams per milliliter. In type 2A, agglutination is essentially flat even at ristocetin concentrations of 1.0 and 2.0, because the high molecular weight multimers needed for platelet binding are missing. Type 2B is the opposite and the key testable pattern, agglutination occurs at abnormally low ristocetin concentrations, as low as 0.2 to 0.5 milligrams per milliliter, well below where normal plasma responds. That's because the type 2B mutation is a gain-of-function change in the A1 domain that causes VWF to bind platelet GPIb spontaneously, even at low ristocetin. This low-dose RIPA hypersensitivity is the classic distinguishing feature of type 2B VWD from platelet-type, or pseudo, VWD, which looks similar but the defect is on the platelet receptor, not VWF itself, and is distinguished using a mixing study with normal platelet-poor plasma.
keypoints: Normal RIPA: dose-dependent agglutination, threshold ~0.8-1.1 mg/mL ristocetin
Type 2A: absent/reduced agglutination even at high ristocetin
Type 2B: enhanced agglutination at LOW ristocetin (<0.6 mg/mL) - hallmark finding
Type 2B mechanism: gain-of-function A1 domain mutation
2B vs platelet-type VWD: mixing study differentiates (plasma vs platelet defect)
keypoint_voiceover: RIPA is dose-dependent in normal plasma. Type 2A shows little to no agglutination even at high ristocetin because HMW multimers are missing. Type 2B is the high-yield pattern, agglutination at low ristocetin concentrations, under about 0.6 milligrams per milliliter, because of a gain-of-function mutation that makes VWF bind platelets spontaneously. When you see enhanced low-dose RIPA, think type 2B versus platelet-type pseudo-VWD, and use a mixing study to tell them apart.
